title: Adjectives and adverbs
tagline: Put adjectives in the right order, choose -ed or -ing, and know when hard becomes hardly.
why: A lovely old wooden box sounds natural; an old lovely wooden box doesn't, and B1 Preliminary examiners expect the right order without thinking. The cloze also loves testing -ed/-ing pairs like bored/boring and sneaky pairs like hard/hardly, where one small change completely changes the meaning.

hook.text: Liam: "That was a really boring film." Sofia: "I know — I was so bored I nearly fell asleep!" Nadia: "At least the beautiful old soundtrack was good. Liam hardly noticed it, though."
hook.ask: Boring and bored look similar but mean different things — which one describes the film, and which one describes how Liam felt? And does hardly mean Liam works hard, or that he barely notices things?

diagrams.title: Put adjectives in the right order
diagrams.caption: Opinion always goes first; the noun's own type or purpose goes right next to it.

rows.label: Meaning
cells: describes the thing that causes the feeling

steps.label: Manner (how): usually after the verb or object
Degree (how much): before the adjective or adverb it describes
Frequency (how often): before the main verb, after be
steps.ex: I usually walk to school. / I'm usually late.

steps.label: so + adjective, such + a/an + adjective + noun
steps.ex: It was so boring. / It was such a boring film.

examples.text: We watched an exciting new film last night.
He wore a smart black jacket to the interview.
That's a tall young actor from the new series.
I was really bored during the maths class.
The match was exciting from start to finish.

examples.note: manner = how — usually after the verb/object
degree = how much — before the adjective

examples.text: Nadia often watches films at the weekend.
examples.note: frequency = how often — before the main verb

examples.text: Mateo studied hard for the test, but he hardly slept.
examples.note: hard = a lot; hardly = almost not at all — very different meanings

examples.text: It was such a good film that we watched it twice.

watch_out.why: Opinion (lovely) comes before fact adjectives like age (old) and material (wooden).
Use -ed for how you feel; -ing describes the thing that causes the feeling.
Adverbs of manner usually need -ly, even after verbs like sing.
hard = a lot of effort; hardly means 'almost not at all' — they aren't related words.
such + a/an + adjective + noun; so is only used with an adjective alone (so good).
good is an adjective; well is the adverb that goes with verbs like drive.

l1.why: Spanish often links adjectives with y in any order; English drops the and and follows a fixed order — opinion first.
Spanish aburrido can suggest both feelings; English needs -ed for the feeling and -ing for the cause.
duro looks like hardly, but the correct adverb is hard — hardly means something completely different.
Spanish bien becomes well with a verb like sing, not the adjective good.

remember.trick: Opinion first, then fact — feelings before facts!
remember.tip: -ED is how YOU feel; -ING is what IT is like. I'm bored because the film is boring.

dialogue.title: Film club review
dialogue.context: Liam, Sofia, Nadia and Mateo just watched a film together and are giving their opinions for the school film club blog.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: That was a really boring film, honestly.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I know — I was so bored I nearly fell asleep!

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: At least the beautiful old soundtrack was good.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I hardly noticed the music, to be honest.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: The main actor was a talented young Peruvian actor, though.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: True. He acted brilliantly in the sad scenes.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: It was such a slow story, that's the problem.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Exactly. I usually love action films, but this one wasn't exciting at all.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Let's write that in the review: an interesting idea, but a disappointingly slow film.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Perfect. And let's watch a really good comedy next time!

items.sentence: I was really ___ during the film.
I ___ watch horror films — I don't like them.
It was ___ good film that we watched it twice.

items.why: well is the adverb, good is the adjective

practice.instructions: Complete with the correct form of the word in brackets, or a suitable word.

items.sentence: I was really ___ (bore) during the film.

practice.instructions: Put the words in order. Tap them one by one.

items.answer: She has a lovely old guitar.
I was really bored during the film.
Mateo hardly slept before the exam.
It was such a boring film.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it means the same as the first, using the word given. Use no more than three words.

items.first: It's an old box, and it's also lovely.
The film made me feel bored.
I felt very bored during the lesson.
Mateo made a big effort when he studied for the exam.
This film is very good — one of the best I've seen.

can_do: I can put two or three adjectives in the right order before a noun.
I can choose between -ed and -ing adjectives correctly.
I can position adverbs of manner, degree and frequency, and use hard/hardly, good/well correctly.
summary: Adjective order: opinion, then size/age/shape, then colour/origin/material, then the noun.
-ed adjectives describe feelings; -ing adjectives describe the thing that causes them.
Adverbs of manner usually go after the verb or object; degree adverbs go before the adjective; frequency adverbs go before the main verb but after be.
hard/hardly, late/lately and good/well are different words, not the same word with -ly added.
so + adjective alone; such + a/an + adjective + noun.
